ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Approval to NCLP for Thane and Solapur 
*421.SHRITARIQ ANWAR: † 
SHRI DATTA MEGHE: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government had accorded approval to the National Child 
Labour Projects under the Child Labour (P&R) Act, 1986 for Thane and 
Solapur in 1995 and for 11 other districts in the years 2003 and 2004; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, the facilities and support provided to child 
labour thereunder and the number of children covered in Maharashtra under 
the scheme; 
(c) whether Government of Maharashtra has proposed some more 
districts in the State to be covered under the National Child Labour Projects; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRA SEKHAR RAO): (a) to (e) A St atement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Tariq 
Anwar. 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2005] 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Under the National Child Labour Project (NCLP) 
Scheme, in addition to Solapur and Thane, 11 more disdtricts of Maharashtra, 
namely, Nanded, Yavatmal, Dhule, Beed, Nasik, Pune, Ahmednagar, Sangli, 
Kolhapur, Jalgaon and Nandurbar have been included under NCLP Scheme in 
the year 2004. Under the National Child Labour Project Scheme, Special 
schools/Rehabilitation Centres are set up, which provide following facilities to 
the children withdrawn from employment: 
Formal/Non-formal education; 
Vocational Training; 
Supplementary nutrition @ Rs. 5/- per child; 
Stipend @ Rs. 100/- per month to children withdrawn from 
employment; 
Health care facilities. 
So far, 3,700 children are being covered under the Scheme in the two 
old districts of Thane and Solapur. Based upon the recommendations of the 
State Government, Nanded, Nasik, Yavatmal and Beed, have been recently 
sanctioned 25, 44, 2 and 25 special schools for child labour respectively in 
the year 2005, which will cover 4800 children. However, in the case of rest of 
the selected districts, namely Dhule, Pune, Ahmadnagar, Sangli, Kolhapur, 
Jalgaon and Nandurbar, the proposals for special schools for Child Labour 
from the State Government are still awaited. 
(c) to (e) The State Government of Maharashtra has submitted 15 
proposals for inclusion of districts under the NCLP Scheme between 1999 to 
2004. The NCLPs are selected by th e Government on the basis of the 
endemicity of child labour as per the census data. The Scheme was being 
implemented in 100 districts till the 9th Plan. It has subsequently been 
expanded, during the 10th Plan, to cover 250 districts in the country, based on 
the census figures of 2001. Accordingly, Pune, Ahmednagar, Sangli, 
Kolhapur, Jalgaon, Nandurbar, Nanded , Nasik, Yavatmal, Dhule and Beed 
have been selected from the State of Maharashtra for implementation of the 
NCLP Scheme.

 DR. T SUBBARAMI REDDY:

(b) if so, whether Government have also started taking stringent action 
against recruiting agencies found guilty of cheating Indians taken to the Gulf 
with promises of employment; 
(c) if so, whether the Minister during his recent visit to UAE, his first 
had feel of condition of Indians had convinced him that unscrupulous 
recruiting agencies were responsible for miseries that some Indians,

48 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVI RAJ CHAVAN): (a) to (d) With a view to curb the 
exploitation of Indian workers going abroad for employment, it has been 
made mandatory w.e.f. f 5.11T2003 for the Recruiting Agents to submit all 
the employment documents, viz. demand letter, power of attorney and 
specimen empbyment contract in original for obtaining emigration clearance. 
Further, in respect of vulnerable categories of workers, i.e. unskilled labour 
and housemaids/domestic workers; and in respect of nine countries, viz. 
Yemen, Lebanon, Libya, Tanzania, Israel, Jordan, Sudan, Kuwait and Brunei, 
these employment documents are required to be attested by the concerned 
Indian Missbn(s). 
Sporadic complaints are received ab out cheating of Indian workers by 
unregistered recruiting agents. On recei pt of such complaints, the concerned 
Protector of Emigrants, (POEs) are dir ected to file complaints/ FIRs against 
such unregistered recruiting agencies for violation of section 10 of the 
Emigration Act 1983. During the years i.e. 2003,2004 and 2005 (upto 
31.07.2005), 25,39 and 33 complaints have respectively been filed with the 
Police authorities against such illegal recruiting agencies. 
Further, with a view to avoid exploitation of workers by unscrupulous 
recruiting agencies, all State Governments/Union Territories have been 
requested to instruct the Police Stations to keep strict vigil on the activities of 
the unregistered agencies engaged in illegal emigration. 
When such complaints are received against registered recruiting agents, 
the concerned recruiting agents is directed  to settle the matter. If he fails to 
do so, action is taken to suspend an d thereafter cancel the registration 
certificate. During the years 2003, 2004 and 2005 (upto 31.07.2005), the 
number of registration certificates suspended was 3,24 and 20 respectively 
and the number of those cancelled was 2, 2 and 13 respectively. 
Apart from recruiting agents, there are also complaints of harassment 
and exploitation by the foreign employers. The Indian Missions intervene in 
all cases that are brought to their notice. 
Further, measures under contemplation include a scheme for providing 
legal assistance through the Indian Missions to Indian workers who are 
advised to file a case before the concerned Ministry of Foreign Government, 
entering into Memorandums of Understanding (Molls) with foreign 
Governments, etc.

3130. SHRI R. KAMARAJ: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state:  
(a) whether it is a fact that Government had asked the Coal India Ltd. 
to expand its capacity of coal exploration; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that th e demand for coal is likely to be 
increased by 20 tonnes in the near future; and 
(d) if so, the steps proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) and (b) Coal India Limited (CIL) is 
conducting coal exploration in CIL non-CIL blocks by drilling about 2 lakh 
metres per year through its subsidiary company i.e. Central Mine Planning & 
Design Institute Limited (CMPDIL). The resources of State Governments 
and Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd. (a public sector undertaking) are 
also utilized in a limited manner for drilling. It has been proposed to increase 
the exploration in non-CIL blocks (captive mining blocks) for which major 
services of agencies other than CMPDIL will also be required. This will 
increase the availability of explored blocks for allocation to prospective 
entrepreneurs for captive mining. 
(c) and (d) The demand of coal by end of 10th Plan and 11 th Plan is 
assessed at 473.18 Million tonnes (as assessed by Planning commission 
during mid-term appraisal),and 676 Million tonnes (as assessed now) 
respectively. As per the plan a produc tion level of 431.50 Million tonnes and 
593 Million tonnes will be achieved by the end of Xth and Xlth Plan period 
respectively. To bridge the gap between demand and availability of coal, 
besides import of coal, following steps have been taken to ensure adequate 
availability of coal: 
(i) Coal India Limited has been asked to increase production form 
existing mines and expedite production from new projects.

mining. Out of these, 86 coal blocks have been allotted/decided for

mining blocks without restriction of captive mining. 
(iv) Exploration for new coal blocks has been expedited. 
(v) Procedure for project approvals has been streamlined.

(b) and (c) It is not possible to compare the production of different

(d) The value of coal produced by Coal India Limited and Singafeni

(e) and (f) The productivity of Indian coal mines do not compare 
favourably with those in other countries. This is because of the fact that large 
scale mechanisation is not feasible due to adverse geo-mining conditions and 
developed pillars in large number of old mines. The method of computation 
of productivity as followed in Indian Coal mines in general is quite different 
from the same followed internationally. In India, persons engaged in services 
like hospital, water supply, sanitation, workshops, watch & ward etc, are 
included in calculating man-shifts employed. In foreign countries, only 
persons engaged directly in production of coal are considered and many 
service jobs done through contractor s are excluded for the purpose of 
computation of productivity.

CIL—

bolding while depillaring.

2. Opencast Mines:— 
• Increase of norms to 330 working days per year against earlier norm 
of 300 days 
• Opening more Greenfield Projects of high capacity to suit

Statement 
Salient Features of Broadband Policy 2004 
1. Definition and Targets: 
Broadband has been defined as and always- on data connection 
supporting interactive se rvices including Intern et access with minimum 
download speed of 256 Kbps per subscriber. The new broadband policy aims 
to target three million broadband subscribers and six million Internet 
99 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2005] 
subscribers with a timeframe of December 2005. By the end of year 2010, the 
policy aims to target 20 million broadband subscribers and 40 million 
Internet subscribers. 
2.0 Technology Options for Broadband Services 
The Broadband Policy Framework visu alizes creation of infrastructure 
through various access technologies whic h can contribute to growth and can 
mutually coexist. Spread of infrastructure is a must for healthy competition 
and therefore it would be the endeavour of the Government that the 
telecommunication infrastructure growth in the country is not compromised 
in any manner. 
2.1 Various access technologies, inter-alia, are: 
(a) Optical Fibre Technologies: 
With the increase in commercial availability of fibre technologies, the 
cost of fibre rollout is approaching the cost of other wired networks. Spread 
of optical fibre networks shall be emphasized keeping in view the long-term 
perspective. 
(b) Digital Subscriber Lines (DSL) on copper loop: 
Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) and Mahanagar Telephone 
Nigam Limited (MTNL) as well as ot her access providers are expected to 
aggressively use their copper loop in frastructure for providing Broadband 
services through this technology. 
Recognising that last mile copper l oop is not a 'bottleneck facility' for 
broadband services, access providers shal l be free to enter into mutually 
agreed commercial arrangements for utilization of available copper loop for 
expansion of broadband services. The owner of local loop shall be free to 
decide the areas in which investment is to be made to upgrade the 
infrastructure for Broadband sevices. The information regarding the areas in 
which Broadband services are being offered by a service provider shall be 
available in the public domain. 
Further, use of brand-name being treated as a part of the value shall be 
permitted in such commercial arrangements. 
Management of BSNL and MTNL has decided to provide 1.5 million 
connections by the end of 2005. The co rporate/work plan of these Public 
Sector Undertakings (PSUs) have been drawn up for this purpose. 
100 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Thereafter, annual plan for expansion of Broadband services by BSNL 
and MTNL will be determined in consultation with them. Aquarterly review 
of their performance by the Government in the Department of 
Telecommunications (DoT) shall be undertaken to evaluate the achievement 
and redefine the future roadmap, if necessary. 
It is hoped that other access servi ces providers would also provide 
broadband connections using their copper in a targeted manner. A 
constructive review of their performance shall also be undertaken. 
(c) Cable TV Network 
Cable TV network can be used as franchisee network of the service 
provider for provisioning Broadband services. However, all responsibilities 
for ensuring compliance of terms and conditions of the licence shall vest with 
the Licensee. The terms of franchise agreement between Licensee and his 
franchisee shall be settled mutually by negotiation between the two parties 
involved: 
(d) Satellite Media 
Very Small Aperture Terminals (VSAT) and Direct-to-Home(DTH) 
services would be encouraged for penetration of Broadband and Internet 
services with the added advantage to serve remote and inaccessible areas. 
Department of Telecommunications, in consultation with the concerned 
Ministries, will soon propose measures in the direction of Open Sky Policy 
for VSAT operators. The role of Depa rtment of Space (DoS) is critical in 
such an endeavour. 
To keep pace with technological advances, throughput and antenna size 
for VSAT shall be periodically reviewed. 
Commercial VSAT service providers having internet service provider 
(ISP) licence shall be permitted use of same hub station and remote station to 
provide Internet service directly to the subscribers. Further, this remote 
station shall be permitted to be used as a distribution point to provide Internet 
services to multiple independent subscr ibers. Necessary amendments in the 
licence agreement shall be carried out immediately. 
DTH service providers shall be pe rmitted to provide Receive Only 
Internet Service after obtaining Intern et Service Providers (ISP) licence from 
Department of Telecommunications. Further, ISP licensees shall 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2005] 
be permitted to allow customers for downloading data through DTH after 
obtaining necessary permission from the competent authority. DTH Service 
providers will also be permitted to provide bidirectional Internet services after 
obtaining VSAT and ISP licence from DoT 
(e) Terrestrial Wireless 
Recognising that terrestrial wire less is another upcoming technology 
platform for Broadband, it has been decided in principle to de-licence 2.40-
2.48 GHz band for low-power outdoor use of non-protection, non-
interference and non-exclusive basis. Necessary notification shall be issued. 
To accelerate penetration of Broadband and Internet, the 5.15-5.35 GHz 
band shall be de-licensed for the indoor use of low power Wi-Fi systems. For 
outdoor use, the band 5.25-5.35GHz shall be de-licensed in consultation with 
DoS and delicensing in the band 5.15-5.25GHz would be considered after the 
process of vacation. Alternative spectrum bands which are not in high usage 
and could be deployed for Broadband services, shall also be explored and 
identified. 
2.2 Quality of Service (QoS) 
TRAI would be requested to prescribe QoS parameters for provisioning 
of broadband service using various access technologies at an early date. 
2.3 Simplification of Standing Advisory Committee on Radio 
Frequency Allocation (SACFA)/Wireless Planning and 
Coordination (WPC) clearance: 
The VSAT operators shall be allowed to start the installation process 
for VSAT terminals after a period of one month of submitting all relevant 
documents to WPC for SACFA/WPC clear ance wherever the total height of 
such installation is less than 5 meters above the rooftop of an authorized 
building. 
In the case of Receive Only VSAT  terminals and DTH with Receive 
Only Internet, no SACFA/WPC clearance will be required wherever the total 
height of such installation is less than 5 meters above the rooftop of an 
authorized building. 
Government have decided that the reference to Wireless in local Loop 
(WLL) in IND49 of National Frequency Allocation Plan (NFAP)-2002 shall 
be deleted to promote use of .ndigenously developed technologies. 
102 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
This would enable service providers, other than basic service operators, to 
use the 1880-1900 MHz band for provision of various services under their 
licence. 
A transparent scheme is being outlined separately for time-bound 
frequency allocation, sitting clearance and wireless licensing by removing the 
cumbersome procedures, computeri zation and by setting predetermined 
standards. 
3.0 Other salient features: 
■ National Internet Exchange of India (NIXI) has been set up by DIT, 
Government of India to ensure that  Internet traffic, originating and 
destined for India, should be routed within India. It is expected that 
NIXI will take appropriate steps for increasing the utilization of 
such facilities. 
■ The Government has assigned a very high priority to indigenous 
manufacture of broadband related equipments and shall endeavour 
to work closely with the concer ned ministries and manufacturers 
associations so that the equipm ents are made available at an 
affordable price. 
■ DOT is conscious of the fact that  Broadband services can reach the 
urban and rural consumers only if se rvices are offered at affordable 
and easy terms. Department of Telecommunications will work out a 
package in consultation with Ministry of Finance and relaed 
Departments as well as concerned service providers to achieve this.

Statement-Ill 
Steps taken by the Government for promotion of Electronics/IT 
Hardware Exports 
1. Approvals for all foreign direct investment upto 100% in the 
Hardware manufacturing sector are under the automatic route. 
2. National Common Minimum Programme (NCMP) of the Government 
emphasises on energizing and sustaining the growth of manufacturing 
industry including IT Hardware. 
3. Peak rate of customs duty is 15%. Customs duty on ITA-1 items (217 
items) has been abolished from 1.3.2005. All goods required in the 
manufacture of ITA-1 items have been exempted from customs duty 
subject to Actual user condition. Customs duty on specified raw 
materials/inputs used for manufacture of electronic components or 
optical fibres/cables is @ 0%. Customs duty on specified capital 
goods used for manufacture of electronic goods is @ 0%. 
4. Excise duty on computers is @ 0%. Microprocessors, Hard Disc 
Drives, Floppy Disc Drives and CD ROM Drives are exempted from 
excise duty. Parts, components an d accessories of mobile handsets 
including cellular phones are exempted from excise duty. 
5. Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme (EPCG) allows import of 
capital goods on payment of 5% customs duty. The export obligation 
under EPCG Scheme can also be fulfilled by the supply of 
Information Technology Agreement (ITA-1) items to the DTA 
provided the realization is in free foreign exchange. 
6. Supplies of Information Technology Agreement (ITA-1) items and 
notified zero duty telecom/electronic items in the Domestic Tariff 
Area (DTA) by Electroni cs Hardware Technology Park (EHTP)/ 
Export Oriented Unit (EOU) units are counted for the purpose of 
fulfillment of positive Net Foreign Exchange Earnings (NFE). 
7. Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are being set up to enable hassle free 
manufacturing and trading for export purposes. Sales from Domestic 
Tariff Area (DTA) to SEZs are being treated as physical 
114 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
export. This entitles domestic supplie rs to Drawback/DEPB benefits, 
CST exemption and Service Tax exemption. 100% Income Tax 
exemption on export profits available to SEZ units for 5 years. 50% 
for next 5 years and 50% of ploughed back profits for 5 years 
thereafter. 
8. Second hand capital goods are freely importable. 
9. EOU/EHTP units are eligible for Income Tax exemption on export 
profits, upto 2010, in terms of Sections 10A and 10B of the Income 
Tax Act. 
10.      To induce more investment for Research and Development activities, 
a weighted deduction of 150% on the sums paid to any university, 
college or an institution or a scientific research association for the 
purposes of scientific, social or statistical research is available.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) The following steps are being taken for expanding 
and improving the telephone network in rural areas: 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2005] 
(i) Provision of support from Universal Service Obligation Fund 
(USOF) for Operation and Maintena nce of existing Village Public

(VPTs) will be provided in 66,822 unconnected villages progressively by 
November, 2007 with an outlay of Rs. 451 crore. This excludes villages

which are to be provided by Digital Satellite Phone Terminals (DSPTs).

UN Convention on Law of the Seas 
3166.   SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRI R.K. ANAND: 
            SHRI SANJAY RAUT: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a  fact that the UN Convention on Law of the Seas 
(UNCLOS) set a 2009 deadline for countries to submit their claims about the 
outer limit of their continental shelf beyond 200 nautical mile Exclusive 
Economic Zone; 
136 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether it is a also a fact that th e UNCLOS requires that, if dispute 
is not settled, the disputed water would be declared international Water; and 
(c) if so, the details of various claims made by India and their status 
with regard to claims of neighouring countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) The United Nations 
Convention on the Law of the Sea 1982 (UNCLOS) is the universally 
recognized regime, which has established a comprehensive framework for the 
regulation of all ocean space. The Convention entered into force on 16 
November, 1994. India is a State Party to the Convention. 
According to the Convention, a st ate has Territorial Waters of 12 
Nautical Miles and an Exclusive Ec onomic Zone of 200 Nautical Miles 
determined in accordance wi th the provisions of th e Convention. As far as 
India is concerned, this is also the position reflected in the Territorial Waters, 
Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 
1976. 
Claims for a Continental Shelf beyond 200 Nautical Miles are to be 
submitted to the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the 
Continental Shelf by 12 May, 2009. 
Collection and examination of neces sary data are underway for the 
purpose of preparing and submitting India's claim for an extended continental 
Shelf to the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, within the 
prescribed timeframe. In case of  any overlapping claim between 
neighbouring countries, the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea 1982, 
provides that the issue should be resolved by these countries bilaterally 
through negotiations.

Cross Border Terrorism 
3173. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the extent to which the cross-bord er terrorism disrupted the peace 
talks between Indian and Pakistan; 
(b) whether Government have detected any terrorist camps on the 
border line of India and Pa kistan and the number of intruders arrested and 
detained in prison at present; and 
(c) the present stage of peace talks? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (c) Government are aware of the 
existence of a number of terrorist training camps in Pakistan and PoK. There 
has been a spurt in the level of infiltration across the Line of Control (LoC) in 
June-July 2005. In 2005 (till July), in Jammu & Kashmir, 37 infiltration bids 
were foiled and 127 terrorists killed in foiled infiltration bids. 
The Government has, in its interaction with Pakistan at all levels, 
continuously stressed the fact that Pakistan has so far not taken any 
significant action to dismantle the infrastructure of support to terrorism, such 
as communications, launching pads, training camps and funding. 
Government is monitoring the situation very closely, and has made it 
clear to Pakistan that the premise on which the present dialogue process 
142 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
is based is the commitment of January 6, 2004 by Pakistan not to permit any 
territory under Pakistan's control to be used to support terrorism in any 
manner. In the Joint Statement made du ring the visit of President Musharraf 
on April 18, 2005, both countries reaffirmed the commitments made in the 
Joint Press Statement of January 6, 2004. 
Significant developments have taken place in India-Pakistan relations 
since April 2003 when India extended the hand of friendship to Pakistan. 
Relations, which were disrupted after the attack on Parliament on December 
13, 2001, have been restored at the level of High Commissioners and 
transport and communication links have resumed. After the January 6, 2004 
commitment of President Musharraf not to permit the territory under 
Pakistan's control to be used to support terrorism in any manner, the 
Composite Dialogue process was resumed and people to people contact 
increased, giving a new impetus and dimension to our relations. Besides, the 
ceasefire along the LoC, Internationa l Border and AGPL (Siachen) which 
came into effect on November 25, 20 03 has held (with some exceptions). 
The first round of the Composite Dialogue on the eight issues — Siachen, Sir 
Creek, Tulbal Navigation Project, Terrorism and Drug Trafficking, 
Economic and Commercial Cooperation, Promotion of Friendly Exchanges, 
Peace and Security, including CBMs and Jammu and Kashmir took place 
from June—August, 2004. The second round of Composite Dialogue Talks 
has been initiated by the Foreign Secret aries' meeting in December 2004 and 
is currently in progress.

Steps for poverty alleviation 
3212. SHRIGIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken during the last five years to alleviate poverty; and 
180 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the details of schemes and programme formulates by Government 
which have been successful? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The Government has adopted a three 
pronged strategy for reducing poverty in the country. It comprises of (i) 
accelerated economic growth with a fo cus on sectors which are employment 
intensive; (ii) human and social development through provision of basic 
minimum services; and (iii) target ed anti poverty programmes. The 
specifically designed anti poverty programmes for generation of both self 
employment and wage employment in rural areas were restructured in 1999-
2000 in order to enhance their efficacy /impact on the poor and improve their 
sustainability. The Swaranjayanti Gr am Swarozgar Yojaoa (SGSY) was 
launched in April, 1999 following the restructuring of the erstwhile Integrated 
Rural Development Programme (IRDP) and its allied programmes with the 
objective of bringing th e assisted poor families (Swarozgaris) above the 
poverty line through the process of social mobilization, capacity building and 
provision of income generating assets. The Jawahar Rozgar Yojana was 
restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) with effect from 1st 
April, 1999 with the aim of creating village infrastructure and generation of 
supplementary wage employment. The Employment Assurance Schemes 
(EAS) was also strengthened w.e.f 1999-2000 to make it the single wage 
employment programme. In addition, the composite multi pronged strategy 
for housing was also operationalised w.e.f. 1999-2000 with the Indira Awaas 
Yojana (IAY) being the major scheme fo r construction of houses to be given 
to the poor, free of cost. In 2002-03 the schemes of Jawahar Gram Samridhi 
Yojana (JGSY) and Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS) were merged 
under the wage employment of Swaranjayanti Gram Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) 
which seeks to provide additional wage employment along with food security 
and infrastructural development in rural areas. From November 2004 the 
National Food for Work Programme is being implemented in 150 most 
backward districts so that generation of supplementary wage employment and 
provision of food security through creation of need based economic, social 
and community assets in these districts is further intensified. 
(b) Evaluation studies of three of the major rural development 
programmes namely SGSY, SGRY and IAY are available but not for the 
Food for Work programme since it has been launched only recently. These 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2005] 
evaluations reveal that the anti pove rty programmes are well targeted and 
have helped in the creation of rural infrastructure. However, there is 
considerable scope to enhance the effi cacy of the programmes. Brief findings 
of the concurrent evaluation of SGSY, SGRY and IAY may be seen at 
Statement. 
Statement 
Brief findings of the Concurrent Evaluation of Swaranjayanti Gram 
Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), Swaranjayanti Gram Rozgar Yojana 
(SGRY) and Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) 
Concurrent evaluation of SGSY—2002-03 
 A concurrent evaluation was conducted to evalua te the performance of 
SGSY and assess the impact of the programme during 2002-03. The main 
findings of the evaluation are: 
• 92.68 per cent of the Swarozgaris belong to BPL families. Women 
constitute 63.81 per cent of the total sample swarozgaris, which is 
considerably higher than the target ed 40 per cent. Swarozgaris from 
the SC/ST category constituted 47.55 per cent of the sample. Only 
2.45 per cent of the total beneficiary samples were found to be 
physically challenged. 
• The average cost of the various individual projects taken up under 
SGSY in different states varies from Rs. 15,893 to Rs. 39,836. 
• The average annual incremental income earned by individuals is Rs. 
8,800 and by groups is Rs. 34,930. 
• 43.36 per cent of the groups reported an increase in savings. 
• 37.24 per cent individual swarozgaris and 15.09 per cent of SHGs 
swarozgaris have crossed the poverty line because of SGSY support. 
• Training for skill development by the District Rural Development 
Agencies (DRDA) is found to be inadequate. Almost all the groups 
need training on improving the quality of their products. 
• 88.67 per cent of individual beneficiaries market their products or 
services on their own. 
182 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Major complaints reported by the district authorities include delay in 
bank procedure and in disbursement of the assistance (50.73 per cent), lack of 
awareness among target group and inadequate infrastructure. 
Concurrent evaluation of SGRY (2003-04) 
The concurrent evaluation of SGRY was carried out to assess its 
success in terms of employment generated and its impact on the poor. In 
addition, the distribution of foodgrains provided under the programme was 
also examined. The main findings are: 
• 77.61 per cent of the works taken up have been completed during 
the year itself. 
• The average number of days of wage employment generated through 
the scheme is 30.52 days. 
• Only 12 per cent of beneficiaries are women, though the scheme 
envisages that at least 30 per cent of wage employment opportunities 
should be reserved for women. 
• The maximum quantity of rice per manday was distributed in 
Andhra Pradesh (6.32 Kg) while beneficiaries in Rajasthan got the 
maximum quantity of wheat (8.96 Kg) 
Concurrent evaluation of IAY 
The Concurrent evalution of the IAY was undertaken in 2001 to assess 
its impact and to examine issues of targeting, functioning of the PRIs and 
quality of assets created. The main findings are: 
• The programme has been able to provide shelter benefits to 
significant proportions of socially and economically vulnerable 
populations in most states. 
• 57 per cent of the beneficiaries belong to the SC category and 22 per 
cent to the ST category. 
• The average annual income of th e beneficiaries at the time of 
selection was Rs. 11,062. 
• 78.16 per cent of the total bene ficiaries were selected by the gram 
sabhas. 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2005] 
• 83 per cent of the houses were constructed on plots owned by the 
beneficiaries. However, only 47 per cent of the houses were 
constructed by beneficiaries themselves. 
• About 50 per cent of the beneficiaries have received assistance in the 
form of cash and the rest in the form of material. 
• 86 per cent of the beneficiaries have expressed their satisfaction with 
constructed houses and the occupancy rate of IAY houses is very 
high. 
• Most of the IAY houses have used local material for construction, 
thus resulting in useful linkages with local skills and resources. 
• In general, the beneficiaries do not feel the assistance is adequate. 
• The ownership titles of the houses are predominantly in the name of 
male family members.

Data regarding Poverty 
3215. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR:  Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether marked disparities have been observed in the data about the 
extent of poverty prevailing in the coun try as per statistics provided by the 
National Sample Survey Organization (NSSO) and the National Account 
Statistics; 
(b) if so, the latest estimates provided by the two organizations about 
the population living Below Poverty Line in urban and rural India, as at the 
beginning and middle of the Tenth Five Year Plan and as per Mid-Term 
Appraisal, State-wise; 
(c) the reasons for the discrepancy; and 
(d) the special steps adopted and being adopted to achieve the Tenth 
Plan targets? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M. V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) to (c) The Planning Commission, as 
the nodal agency to estimate the extent of poverty prevailing in the country, 
does not estimate poverty from National Accounts Statistics data. It estimates 
poverty only from the data generated by the large sample survey on 
'Household Consumer Expenditure' conducted by NSSO at an interval of 
approximately five years following the recommendations of the Expert Group 
on 'Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor' (Lakdawala Committee). 
To the best of Government's knowledge, no estimates about the extent of 
poverty prevailing in the country are made only on the basis of the NAS. 
Therefore, the issue of marked disparities in the data and the extent of 
poverty as estimated from the National Sample Survey Organization (NSSO) 
and the National Accounts Statistics (NAS) does not arise. 
However, there is divergence in 'private final consumption expenditure' 
estimated from NSS Survey data and National Accounts Statistics data. 
186 
 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The Total Household Consumption Expenditure estimated from the latest 
large sample survey conducted in 1999-2000 (NSS 55th Round) was Rs. 
707151.9 crore, whereas the Private Final Consumption Expenditure 
according to National Accounts Sta tistics during 1999-2000 was Rs. 
1271556.00 crore in current prices. The difference between the two estimates 
of 'private final consumption expenditure' is due to the different 
methodologies and concepts taken into account by NSS Survey and National 
Accounts Statistics. 
The latest estimates of poverty are available only for 1999-2000, for 
which data exists from the 55th Round of NSSO Survey on Household 
Consumer Expenditure. This is given in Statement. [Refer to the Statement , 
appended to Unstarred Question No. 3208 Part (a) and (b)]. 
(d) The monitorable targets for th e Tenth Five Year Plan include 
quantitative targets for redu ction in the incidence of poverty, according to 
which poverty was projected to be reduced by 5 percentage points by the end 
of the Tenth Plan period. The Government has adopted a three pronged 
strategy to reduce poverty. These are (i) acceleration of economic growth 
with a focus on sectors which are em ployment intensive; (ii) human and 
social development through provision of basic minimum services; and (iii) 
targeted antipoverty programmes. 
There are several steps being taken by Ministry of Rural Development 
and Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation to reduce the 
number of people living below poverty line in rural and urban areas. For 
rural areas the programmes are (i) Swar njayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (ii) 
Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana ( iii) Indira Awaas Yojana and (iv) 
National Food for Work Programme. For urban areas the programme is 
Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojana. In addition, the coverage of 
Antyodaya Anna Yojana has been expanded from 2.0 crore (BPL) families to 
2.5 crore (BPL) families. The National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill 
has also been tabled in Parliament on 21.12.2004.

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Commercialization of Research 
3217. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJ ARY: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are considering to allow 
commercialization of technological and scientific research being carried by 
Indian science institutes and universities; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard; 
(c) whether it is a fact that there is dearth of scientists and other 
professional in major research institutes in the country; 
(d) if so, the details in this regard; and 
(e) the steps proposed to be taken to attract and retain the required 
talent? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Several schemes 
have been put in place by Governme nt to allow commercialization of 
technological and scientific research being carried by Indian science institutes 
and universities by providing infrastruc tural and operational support through 
various schemes and incentives. With increased emphasis on public-private 
partnership in technology development, the Government, through schemes of 
Technology Development Board (T DB), New Millennium Indian 
Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) and Drug & Development 
Promotion Board (DDPB), provides ince ntives to commercialize inventions, 
as these schemes take adequate care to ensure that inventions from scientific 
institutions and universities become an important component of the schemes. 
Ministry of Science and Technology a nd Department of Ocean Development 
allow institutions and universities implementing projects awarded by them to 
own intellectual property rights emanating from such projects and retain 
benefits and earnings accrued from pa tents. Institutions may determine the 
share of inventors and other persons from actual earnings. However, such 
share shall be limited to one-third of the actual earnings. Similar schemes are 
available to the scientists from CSIR and ICAR. 
The Government has set up specialized cells/centers/untis in its different 
departments and agencies which provide technical, financial and legal help to 
scientists for protecting their inventive work in India and, 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2005] 
other countries. Intellectual property rights, so generated, are also maintained 
by these cells/centers/units. The owners hip of such patents resides with the 
concerned institutions and the scientists ' names appear as inventors in the 
patent document. Prominent among the Government Departments/agencies 
are: Department of Science and Technology, Department of Biotechnology, 
Ministry of Telecommunications and information Technology, Department of 
Atomic Energy, Defence Research and Development Organization (DRDO), 
Council of Scientific & Industrial Res earch (CSIR), ISRO, Indian Council of 
Medical Research (ICMR), Indian Coun cil of Agricultural Research (ICAR), 
Indian Council of Forest Research (IC FR). In addition, many awards and 
fellowships have been instituted for re cognizing meritorious scientists and 
giving them incentives to take on R& D projects. There are tax incentives 
available for commercializing indigenously-developed technology. 
(c) to (e) Views have been expressed at various fora, indicating that the 
country is likely to face shortage of scientists in basic sciences, as a result of 
the declining interest in science amongst the young students, lack of sufficient 
incentives, etc. Taking note of these concerns, the Government, in order to 
attract students and researchers and to improve the quality of research, has 
taken various measures by introducing a set of new initiatives. These include 
programmes like "Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Fellowships"—targeted at post-
graduate talented students, "CSIR Diamond Jubilee Technology Awards"—
for innovators for developing technology of the highest benchmarks of 
competitiveness and excellence and for inventions of school students, 
"Women Scientists Scheme"—instituted to provdie opportunities to women 
scientists, "Swarnajayanti Fellowship" —for outstanding young scientists, 
Post-doctoral Fellowship in Biotechnology, Bioscience Awards for career 
development. "Ramanna Fellowship"—aimed to support performing 
scientists, Fund for improvement of infrastructure for S&T in Universities 
and. Higher Educational Institutions, etc. More recently, Government has also 
announced two National Research Fellowship, namely, "Ramanujam 
Fellowships"—to attract brilliant scientists from all over the world and "JC 
Bose Fellowship"—to recognize active scientists who have proven 
outstanding track record. All these initiatives are aimed at providing 
encouragement to scientists. The Government has also instituted several S&T 
programmes with other countries to build international academic and research 
linkages in pure sciences.

Embryonic Stem Cell Research 
3218. PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that US President George 
Bush had taken the view on 9th August, 2001 that embryonic Stem Cell 
Research is the leading edge of a seri es of moral hazards and he would be 
banning federal funding for the research; and 
(b) what is the position of Government of India on this question? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes, Sir. On Aug. 9,2001, 
in the first major speech of his pres idency, Mr. Bush announced that he 
would permit taxpayer financing so long as the studies invovled only those 
stem-cell lines already in existence at that time. The President said he did not 
want to encourage the destruction of any more embroys.The President's 
spokeperson Mr. Duffy had clarified that a fundamental moral line should not 
be crossed by encouraging the destruction of human. 
(b) In India, embryonic stem cell research is being carried out as per the 
existing policy that stem cell research should be promoted in view of its 
potential for clinical use. For embryonic stem cell research, embroys should 
not be generated for the sole purpose of obtaining stem cells. Only surplus, 
spare or supernumerary embroys can be used after obtaining informed 
consent of both spouses. Such collection of embryos should be done only 
from registered Assisted Reproductive Technique (ART) clinics.

Rules made by Governing body of CSIR 
3221. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Governing Body of CSIR has the powers to 
formulate its own rules being an Autonomous body for its Scientific and 
Technical Staff as well as Administrative Staff; 
(b) if so, whether any new and specific rules have been framed by the 
Governing Body of CSIR which are not in conformity with Government 
rules; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes Sir. As per provisions 
of CSIR Rules, Regulations bye-laws 11 and 15, the Governing Body of 
CSIR has the power to formulate its own rules relating to recruitment, 
promotion including assessment and merit promotion in respect of categories 
of scientific and technical staff of the Society. Rule 15 ibid provides that the 
service of the employees of the Societ y shall be governed by Fundamental 
and Supplementary Rules of the Government of India and orders issued 
thereunder to the extent applicable to the employ ees of the Society. The 
Ministry of Finance is represented on the Governing Body through Secretary, 
Expenditure as Member (Finance) to ensure that the power to relax the 
requirement of any rule by the Governing Body is within the permissible 
limit keeping in view the functional requirement and peculiar needs of an 
R&D organization. The proceedings of the Governing Body are approved by 
the Vice President, CSIR (Minister of Science & Technology) and the 
President, CSIR (Prime Minister of India). 
(b) and (c) The Governing Body has framed CSIR Recruitment and 
Promotion Rules including Assessment and Merit Promotion Rules in respect 
of scientific and technical staff.  The Assessment Promotion Rules for 
granting promotion to scientists and technical personnel is in operation from 
1966. The scheme was evolved for giving impetus to R&D effort. The 
Assessment Promotion Scheme in vogue in CSIR for scientific and technical 
staff is broadly similar to that operating in most of the Government 
196 

[25 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
scientific departments. The larger coverage of employees of S&T staff in the 
scheme has been done with a view to attracting best talent at all levels 
(including technical support staff) in the interest of research and 
developmental work. In respect of non-technical posts, recruitment & 
promotion rules i.e. CSIR Administrative Services (Recruitment & 
Promotion) Rules, 1982 are more or less on the pattern of Government of 
India Rules. Slight deviations like relaxation in the residency period due to 
non-availability of eligible candidates in the feeder cadre have been made 
with the approval of the Governing Body, CSIR keeping in view the 
functional requirements and interests of the organization. The rules are 
updated/ revised from time to time with the approval of the Governing Body.

3243. SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN: Will the Minister of SHIPPING

†3277. SHRI DARA SINGH CHAUHAN: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a)the details of sports complexes located in Eastern Uttar Pradesh; 
(b)whether Government are considering to construct well-equipped

(c) if so, the places where they would be constructed and names of

Postponement of Assam Games 
3278. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the National Games to beheld in Assam has 
been postponed from the scheduled date; 
(b) if so, the reasons for that postponement and by when the new date 
for the said game is likely to be rescheduled; and 
(c) if so, the progress achieved by  the State Government for the 
National Games, so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) As informed by the State Government, the Games have been 
postponed due to non-completion of infrastructure including Games Village; 
the delay in completion of these projects is stated to be unprecedented floods 
in Guwahati during 2004 and due to various court cases with regard to Games 
Village. The fresh dates for the Games will be fixed by Indian Olympic 
Association in consultation with Assam Olympic Association and the State 
Government of Assam. 
(c) The State Government of Assam ha s informed that 68% work in 
respect of sports infrastructure has been completed and the State Government 
is expecting to take over these by 31.10.2005. Similarly the State Government 
is expecting to take over the Games Village by December, 2005. Other 
ancillary works are also expected to be completed by the end of December 
2005.

THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, Government has ta ken decisive and effective steps for 
saving the National Textile Corporation (NTC), a sick company from 
liquidation. Due to the initiative taken by the Government, BIFR has approved 
rehabilitation schemes for the NTC companies costing Approximately Rs.3900 
crore. The Government has committed to carry out capital restructuring 
costing nearly Rs.6000 crore. Accordin gly, these rehabilitation schemes are 
under implementation since April, 2002. 
As per the rehabilitation schemes, 66 unviable mills are to be closed 
and 53 potentially viable mills are to be revived with the sale proceeds of 
surplus assets. After un-encumbering the assets, NTC started the process of

Bulk of resources for rehabilitation are to be generated through sale 
of lands in Mumbai. The Government of Maharashtra has amended the 
Regulation 58 of Development Control Regulations for Greater Mumbai, 1991, 
which facilitated sale of the NTC mill land in Mumbai for development of crucial 
civil infrastructure. 
Out of the 25 NTC mills in Mumbai, 39.42 acre land in five mills are to 
be handed over to MHADA/BMC as per the DCR 58 (modified), five mills have 
no surplus lands, and there are 137.04 acre surplus land in the remaining 
fifteen mills in Mumbai. 
In accordance with the scheme finalised by BIFR, NTC has filed 
application before the Commissioner, BMC in May 2003, who is the competent 
authority under the Regulation 58 of Development Control Regulations 
governing the sale of Textile Mills land. Instead of giving permission for sale of 
land, the BMC constituted a sub-committ ee to advise in the matter. The sub-
committee, in its report, suggested for fu rther modification in the Development 
Control Regulations (although the curr ent DC Regulations were promulgated 
after due public notice). The Government of Maharashtra, however, has not 
acted upon the above recommendations  for further modification of the 
Development Control Regulations. 
After vigorous persuasions, the Government of Maharashtra has 
given permission for sale of five mills having 47.69 acres land in the first 
phase. These five mills are - Jupiter, Mumbai, Apollo, Kohinoor 3 and 
Elphinstone. 
In the meanwhile, a self-styled Bombay Environmental Action Group 
(BEAG) of Mumbai filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay against the 
sale of NTC mills' lands. The High Court had granted an interim stay on the 
sale in April, 2005. As it would have violated the directi ons of the Supreme 
Court and made the rehabilitation schemes approved by BIFR non-
implementable, this order was contes ted by NTC in the Supreme Court, 
whereupon the hon. Court on 11.05.2005, vacated the stay orders of High 
Court and permitted NTC to go ahead with the sale of land. 
The NTC has concluded sale of afor ementioned five properties for a 
total amount of Rs.2021 crores. This amount would be used to return the 
amount borrowed from the market to give VRS in NTC (SM/MN) and also to 
meet the cost of modernisation. Apar t from this, NTC (HC) has advanced 
amounts for meeting cash losses which also need to be reimbursed.

this Bill and I have seen the responses from my colleagues in this House. 
Thirty-three Members have spoken. Majority of them have spoken and shared 
with us what they are going through and what they expect from the hon. 
Minister and the Government to do for them. The need is very genuine and 
everybody has heard the various Members explaining how exactly they are 
meeting the two ends. 
Now, four Members have opposed the Bill for various reasons. For 
example, Shri Jairam Ramesh though t, being an economist, that there was no 
need and it was a wasteful expenditure  on the Members of Parliament. He 
must be having his own reasons. I don't think that those reasons are • good 
enough to deprive a Member, who is going through such agony and misery 
that he is not able to conduct and do his duty as a Member of Parliament, what 
is due to him. Our colleague, Shri Dipankar Mukherjee, has a different view

Signing of Memorandum of Understanding on Ken-Betwa Link 
THE MINISTER OF WATER R ESOURCES (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): Sir, the great son of India, former Union Irrigation Minister, late 
Dr. K.L. Rao, dreamt of linking the rivers  of the country. However, it could not 
materialise. The late Prime Minister, B harat Ratna, Smt. Indira Gandhiji did 
not allow the dream of Dr. K.L. Rao to die. In 1980, under her leadership, the 
National Perspective Plan was conceived envisaging transfer of water from 
surplus basins to deficit basins and in 1982, the Central Government, through 
a Resolution, constituted a society known as the National Water Development 
Agency (NWDA). To study the feasibility of  the interlinking of rivers proposals 
suggested in the NPP. The late Prime Minister, Smt. Indira Gandhiji desired 
to identify the links both in the Himalayan and in the Peninsular Zones and 
directed NWDA to take a leading role. The NWDA began their task of 
identifying the links since late 1980s and identified 30 links, 16 under 
Peninsular component and 14 under Himalayan component for preparation of 
feasibility reports in line with the pr oposal of NPP. Meanwhile, during a 
hearing in a PIL in the hon. Suprem e Court during the tenure of the NDA 
Government on a different issue of Yamuna river's pollution, the amicus curie 
requested the hon. Court to give 
357 

RAJYA SABHA [25th August, 2005] 
a direction to the Central Government to consider the networking of rivers. The 
hon. Court directed to treat this issue as an independent PIL with cause title 
'Networking of Rivers' and directed the Centre and States to respond. 
Accordingly, the NDA Government headed by the then hon. Prime 
Minister, Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayeeji, formed a Task Force, headed by the 
hon. Member of Lok Sabha, Shri Suresh Prabhu.  The Task Force submitted  
their Report on time, but could not ev olve consensus amongst the political 
leadership of the country together or  for any link bilaterally. The UPA 
Government, in their Common Minimum Programme, gave special emphasis, 
based on discussion and decision, in a fully consultative manner to identify 
and confine the linking policy within the peninsular zone. 
Accordingly, within the completion of first year of the UPA 
Government, we have finally concluded the Memorandum of Understanding 
between two States, after prolonged negotiations at various levels, that is, 
Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh to have the Detailed Project Report of 
Ken-Betwa link, which is the first river link of India. Uttar Pradesh had some 
definite reservations on certain issues which they would like to address at the 
DPR stage. This is a hist oric decision and a step forward to fulfil the dream of 
late Dr. K.L Rao and the architect of t he National Perspective Plans, late Smt. 
Indira Gandhiji, through the sustained efforts of the UPA Government. 
The Ken-Betwa link proposal will be nefit both the States in their 
districts, namely, Chhatarpur, Tikam garh, Panna, Raisen and Vidisha in 
Madhya Pradesh and Hamirpur, Jhansi and Banda in Uttar Pradesh by way of 
increased and stabilised irrigation, conse quent increase in the production of 
food and commercial crops, improved avai lability of drinking water, flood and 
drought mitigation and other increased ec onomic activities like pisciculture, 
afforestation, tourism, generation of hydropower and ecological improvement 
programmes. This link will ensure an overall development of the region. 
I thank the engineers and technicians of NWDA, which began its 
journey in 1982 under the leadership of Mrs. Gandhi. I profoundly thank the 
hon. Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singh, for his sustained intervention and 
interest in this matter. It is needless to mention that to implement the Common 
Minimum Programme's one of the key issue the initiative and support of the 
Chairperson of the National Advisory Council, Smt. Sonia

and consent for the Detailed Project Report, based on this Memorandum of
